title: All the flowers (ch. 1)
hookLine: everyone online looks like a rose; Thérèse asks why God gives some souls more, and answers with a garden
tomorrow: what changed the happy little girl when she was four?

lines: WHY SOME SOULS, AND NOT OTHERS?
cards: Scroll for five minutes and everybody looks like a rose: the acceptance letter, the starting spot, the perfect family photo.
Thérèse had her own version of that feeling, and she asks it straight out on the first pages of her notebook. Why does God seem to give some souls so many graces, and others so few?
Why great saints, and then souls nobody notices? Her answer came from a garden.

teach.h: THE ROSE TAKES NOTHING FROM THE DAISY.
teach.b: Jesus, she writes, set the book of nature in front of her. The splendor of the rose and the whiteness of the lily don't take away the scent of the little violet or the plain charm of the daisy.
If every small flower wanted to be a rose, nature would lose its springtime dress. That, she says, is the world of souls, Jesus's garden.
He made great saints, like lilies and roses, and smaller ones, glad to be daisies or violets. Perfection is doing his will, being what he wants us to be.

teach.h: ONE SUN, AS IF EACH WERE ALONE.
teach.b: And the same sun lights the tall cedar and each tiny flower as if each were alone on earth. A daisy isn't a failed rose. It's a daisy, on purpose.
A neighbor tradition has its own way of saying each person is made on purpose. The Mishnah, an early collection of Jewish teaching, asks why humanity began with one single person.
One reason it gives: so no one could ever say to another, my ancestor was greater than yours. And it adds an image.

teach.h: THE MISHNAH: ONE SEAL, NO TWO ALIKE.
teach.b: A king stamps many coins with one seal, and they all come out alike.
God stamped every human being with the seal of the first person, and not one is like another. One family, no two the same.

The honest difference: the Mishnah says it to show the worth of every human life, and to stop anyone ranking ancestors. Thérèse is speaking of graces and holiness, and her garden does hold greater and smaller flowers.
She's simply glad to be small.

how: Catholics call Thérèse the Little Flower, and her flower image from these opening pages is part of Catholic devotion to her.

o: only the great saints really count to God
each soul is loved as it is, great or small
every soul must become the same kind of saint

games.q: all the flowers — tap the pairs.
p: smaller souls, glad to be small

s: Thérèse says the small souls are second-rate in God's garden
the rose takes nothing from the daisy; each is made on purpose.
the Mishnah says humanity began with one person so no one could say 'my ancestor was greater'
one family, and every face stamped differently.
Thérèse says every soul should try to become a rose
if every flower wanted to be a rose, nature would lose its springtime dress.

games.q: at a school assembly on one human race, a classmate says every religion secretly teaches the same thing. what's the honest reply from today?
o: some ideas truly meet, like each person made on purpose, and real differences remain.
yes: Thérèse's garden and the Mishnah's coins mean exactly the same thing.
no: a Catholic saint and the Mishnah have nothing in common at all.
games.why: both see each person as made on purpose, no copies. but the Mishnah speaks of the worth of every human life; Thérèse speaks of graces and holiness.

practice: Find one small living thing near you, a leaf, a weed in a sidewalk crack, a houseplant, or a photo of a flower, and look at it as if it were the only one on earth. If you pray, you can rest in the words thy will be done.

wordCard.voice: All the flowers. Thérèse's garden of souls: roses and lilies, daisies and violets, each one made on purpose.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: every flower, and a daisy is not a smaller rose. Be well today.
